title: React
summary: Seventeen skills cover nearly all day-to-day React work; everything else you learn on the job when a ticket needs it.

skip.item: Class components, componentDidMount and other lifecycle methods
skip.why: New code is all function components; you can learn to read a class in one afternoon if a job needs it
Vite and frameworks configure this for you

skip.instead: TanStack Query for server data, Zustand for client state; Redux Toolkit only if a job lists it

skip.item: fetch inside useEffect in real apps
skip.why: Race conditions, no caching, no retries
skip.instead: TanStack Query or framework data loading (you'll try the raw way once in Week 3)
Profile first; know the hooks for interviews

skip.why: Since React 19, ref is a normal prop on function components

skip.item: Deep dives on Fiber and the diffing algorithm
skip.instead: One paragraph: render, then commit; keys help React match list items

modules.title: Components, JSX, props, lists
modules.goal: By Friday you can turn any static screenshot into a tree of React components fed by data.
learn: Scaffold with Vite: npm create vite@latest week1 -- --template react, then npm run dev. Know what index.html, main.jsx and App.jsx each do.
JSX rules: one root element or <> fragment, className, {} for any JavaScript expression, self-closing tags.
Components are functions that return JSX. PascalCase names, one per file.
Props: destructure them, pass children for layout wrappers, never mutate them.
Lists: .map() with a stable key (an id, not the array index).
Conditional rendering: &&, the ternary, and early return.
Keep components pure: same props in, same JSX out, no side effects while rendering.
Install React DevTools in your browser and inspect every component you write.

build.title: Product catalogue page
build.brief: Hard-code a JSON array of 12 products. Render a responsive grid of ProductCard components with a "Sale" badge when discounted, an "Out of stock" state, and a Layout component that wraps the page with children. Push it to GitHub and deploy it free on Vercel or Netlify.

doneWhen: You can sketch a component tree from any web page in under 10 minutes
You can explain why index keys break when a list is reordered
The console shows zero key warnings
The catalogue is live at a public URL

modules.title: State, events, forms
modules.goal: By Friday you can build any interactive widget and decide, without guessing, which component should own each piece of state.
learn: useState: state is a snapshot per render; use the updater form setCount(c => c + 1) when the next value depends on the last.
Events: onClick, onChange, onSubmit with e.preventDefault().

Immutable updates, the patterns you'll type daily: Object: setUser({ ...user, name }); Add: setItems([...items, item]); Remove: setItems(items.filter(i => i.id !== id)); Update: setItems(items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i))
Controlled inputs: text, checkbox, select and textarea bound to state.
Lifting state up: move state to the closest common parent and pass callbacks down.
Derive, don't store: compute filtered lists and totals during render instead of keeping them in extra state.
useReducer when several state values change together (cart, multi-step form).

build.title: Expense tracker
build.brief: Add, edit and delete expenses; filter by category and month; show a running total and per-category totals (derived, not stored). Use useReducer for the expense list. This is the Foundations gate: rebuild it from a blank project without notes.

doneWhen: You can explain why setCount(count + 1) called three times only adds one
Every array and object update in your code is immutable
You rebuilt the tracker from scratch in under 3 hours

modules.title: Effects, refs, custom hooks, Context
modules.goal: By Friday you can talk to an API, share logic through your own hooks, and, just as important, recognise when an effect is the wrong tool.
learn: Effects sync React with things outside it: timers, subscriptions, browser APIs, network. Master the dependency array and the cleanup function.
When not to use an effect: derived data (compute it during render) and logic caused by a click (put it in the handler). This is the most common code-review comment on junior React code.
Strict Mode runs effects twice in development on purpose; it exposes missing cleanup.
Fetch the raw way once: loading/error/data states, plus AbortController to cancel stale requests. Feel the pain; Week 5 removes it.
useRef: focus an input, hold a timer id, keep a value that shouldn't trigger a render.
Custom hooks: useDebounce, useLocalStorage. Follow the rules of hooks (top level only, names start with use).
Context for app-wide, rarely changing values (theme, signed-in user). Since React 19 you render <ThemeContext value={...}> directly instead of .Provider.
Keep eslint-plugin-react-hooks on (the Vite template ships it); it catches dependency bugs.

build.title: Weather search
build.brief: Search any city with a debounced input (your useDebounce), show a 7-day forecast with loading, error and empty states, cancel stale requests with AbortController, save favourite cities with your useLocalStorage, add a dark-mode toggle through Context, and autofocus the search box with useRef.

doneWhen: You can name three situations where an effect is the wrong tool
Typing fast never shows results for an old query
Each custom hook is used by at least two components

modules.title: TypeScript for React + React Router
modules.goal: By Friday your apps are typed end to end and have real URLs, the two things that separate tutorial code from team code. From here on, every project starts with --template react-ts.
learn: Only the TypeScript React needs: type vs interface, unions ('idle' | 'loading' | 'error'), optional fields, arrays, and enough generics to read useState<User | null>(null).
Type props (with children: React.ReactNode), events (React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>), refs (useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)), context and API responses.
Extend native elements: type ButtonProps = React.ComponentProps<'button'> & { variant: 'primary' | 'ghost' }.
Model UI states with discriminated unions so "loading and error at once" can't happen.
Start in Declarative mode: <BrowserRouter>, <Routes>, <Route>, <Link>/<NavLink>.
useParams for /expenses/:id, useNavigate after a form submit, useSearchParams to keep filters in the URL.
Nested routes with an <Outlet> layout, a 404 route, and a protected-route wrapper that redirects with <Navigate>.
Know that Data mode (loaders and actions) and Framework mode exist; read the comparison once and move on.

build.title: Typed, multi-page expense tracker
build.brief: Migrate your Week 2 tracker to TypeScript with strict on (migrating JS to TS is a real on-the-job task). Add routes /expenses, /expenses/:id, /reports, /settings and /login; keep filters in the URL; gate everything except /login behind a fake auth user held in Context.

doneWhen: tsc passes in strict mode with zero any
Refreshing any URL, including a filtered list, restores the same screen
A logged-out user hitting /reports is sent to /login, then back to /reports

modules.title: Server state, forms, styling, global state
modules.goal: This is the week that makes you employable: by Friday you can build the CRUD dashboard that most frontend tickets live inside.
learn: The core idea: server state (data that lives on a server and goes stale) is different from client state (UI-only). Different tools for each.

TanStack Query v5: QueryClientProvider, useQuery with a queryKey, staleTime, isPending/isError; useMutation then invalidateQueries; pagination with placeholderData: keepPreviousData; one optimistic update; the Devtools panel.
React Hook Form + Zod: useForm, register, handleSubmit, formState.errors, zodResolver. Use z.infer<typeof schema> so one schema gives you both validation and the TypeScript type.
Tailwind CSS: flex and grid utilities, spacing scale, responsive prefixes (md:), dark mode.
shadcn/ui: copy-in components (Button, Dialog, Table, Form, toasts) built on accessible primitives. You own the code, so read it.
Zustand: one small store for client state (sidebar open, table density), read through selectors. Learn Redux Toolkit only if a job you want lists it.

build.title: Inventory admin dashboard (the Real-app gate)
build.brief: A products table with search, sort and pagination from json-server; create and edit in a shadcn Dialog with React Hook Form + Zod; delete with a confirm step and an optimistic update; toast on every mutation; sidebar state in Zustand; responsive with dark mode.

doneWhen: No useEffect fetches remain anywhere in the app
Saving an edit updates the table without a manual refetch
One Zod schema drives both validation and the TypeScript type
The layout works at 375 px and 1440 px wide

modules.title: Testing, performance, errors, accessibility, CI
modules.goal: By Friday your dashboard is something a team would merge: tested, fast, accessible, and checked by CI on every push.
learn: Testing: Vitest + React Testing Library + user-event. Query the way users see the page (getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }), getByLabelText), use findBy for async UI, and test behaviour, not implementation.
Mock the network with MSW so tests hit fake endpoints instead of stubbing fetch.
What to test first: a form's validation errors, a list rendering API data, one mutation's happy path. Ten meaningful tests beat chasing 100% coverage.

Performance: find slow renders with the React DevTools Profiler; turn on React Compiler instead of hand-adding useMemo/useCallback/memo; split routes with lazy + <Suspense>. Still know the manual hooks: interviewers ask.
Errors: an error boundary around each route (the react-error-boundary package) so one crash doesn't blank the app.
Accessibility: semantic HTML, a label on every input, full keyboard use, visible focus. Run Lighthouse and fix what it flags.
CI: a GitHub Actions workflow running lint, tsc and tests on every push; environment variables through import.meta.env.VITE_*.

build.title: Harden the Week 5 dashboard
build.brief: Add 10+ tests using MSW, React Compiler, lazy-loaded routes, an error boundary per route, and a GitHub Actions workflow with a passing badge in the README. Fix every Lighthouse accessibility issue.

doneWhen: A pull request with a failing test is blocked by CI
Lighthouse accessibility scores 90 or higher
You can show a before/after Profiler recording and explain the difference

modules.title: Next.js App Router + React 19
modules.goal: By Friday you can build full-stack React with Next.js 16, the framework most React job posts name alongside React itself. Everything from Weeks 1–6 still applies; the new idea is where code runs.
learn: File-based routing: app/page.tsx, layout.tsx, dynamic [id] folders, and the special files loading.tsx, error.tsx, not-found.tsx.

Server Components are the default: they can be async and read data directly. Add 'use client' only where you need state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs, and push it down to the smallest component.
Mutations with Server Functions ('use server', which Next.js calls Server Actions), then revalidatePath to refresh the page's data.
React 19 form hooks: useActionState for result + pending state, useFormStatus for submit buttons, useOptimistic for instant UI.
Validate with Zod again on the server; never trust the client.
Route handlers (app/api/.../route.ts) when something outside your UI needs a REST endpoint.
SEO and polish: the Metadata API, next/image, next/font.
Caching defaults changed in Next.js 16; trust the current docs over older videos on this topic.

build.title: Port the dashboard to Next.js
build.brief: Days 1–3: finish the official Next.js Learn course, typing every line. Days 4–5: port your inventory dashboard's list, detail and create/edit pages to Next.js with Server Actions and useActionState, and deploy to Vercel with a free Postgres database. This closes the Production gate.

doneWhen: You can say in one sentence when a component needs 'use client'
A form submits through a Server Action and shows pending state and field errors
The app runs on Vercel against a real database

modules.title: Capstone – Job Application Tracker
modules.goal: Build a full-stack SaaS-style job application tracker: sign in, log every application, drag it across a Kanban board, and see your hiring funnel. Every hiring manager understands it in five seconds, and it uses every skill from Weeks 1–7. Give it your own name.

build.title: Job application tracker (MVP)
build.brief: Build a full-stack SaaS-style job application tracker: sign in, log every application, drag it across a Kanban board, and see your hiring funnel. Every hiring manager understands it in five seconds, and it uses every skill from Weeks 1–7. Give it your own name.
checklist: Sign up and log in with email or GitHub via Supabase Auth; each user sees only their own rows.
Create, edit and delete applications: company, role, job link, location, salary range, status, applied date, notes.
Kanban board with Wishlist, Applied, Interview, Offer and Rejected columns; dragging a card updates status optimistically.
Table view with search, status filter and date sort, all kept in the URL.
Responsive layout, dark mode, and a loading, empty and error state on every screen.

doneWhen: The live URL is on your resume, LinkedIn and GitHub profile README
You can walk through the architecture and defend three decisions in 5 minutes
A stranger can sign up and use it without asking you anything

topics.title: JSX, components, props
topics.why: Break every screen into reusable pieces that pass data down
topics.summary: Split a screen into components: functions that take props and return JSX, nest like HTML, and get their data from their parent.
objectives: Write a component as a function that takes props and returns JSX, following the JSX rules
Pass data down with props, including `children` for wrapper components, without ever changing them
Break a page into a tree of small components that each do one job

examples.title: Props with a default
examples.takeaway: Destructuring in the parameter list names the props the component reads, a default fills in `size` when the parent leaves it out, and `style` takes an object.

examples.title: Wrapping content with children
examples.takeaway: Whatever sits between `<Card>` and `</Card>` arrives as `children`, so one `Card` can wrap any content.

examples.title: A page as a tree of components
examples.takeaway: Data starts at the top and flows down through props; each component knows only the props it is given.

resources.note: What a component is, how to write one and how to nest them.
Props in depth: destructuring, defaults, `children`, and why they are read-only.
The whole first chapter of the React docs, with small challenges after each page.
How to turn a design into a tree of components, and decide where each piece of data lives.
An interactive course, if you learn best by typing along with a video.

topics.title: Lists with keys, conditional rendering
topics.why: Render API results, plus empty, loading and error states
topics.summary: Turn arrays into lists with map and stable keys, and show the right thing for every state: loading, error, empty and loaded.
objectives: Render an array with `map`, giving every item a stable, unique `key` from the data
Explain what goes wrong when the array index is the key and the list changes
Show loading, error, empty and loaded states with early returns, the ternary and `&&`

examples.title: Keys that come from the data
examples.takeaway: `key={todo.id}` follows each todo wherever it moves, so a ticked checkbox stays with its own item when the list is sorted or filtered.

examples.title: Every state, with early returns
examples.takeaway: Each early return handles one state, so the `map` at the end only runs when there is something to show.

examples.title: The 0 trap with &&
examples.takeaway: Make the left side of `&&` a real boolean, such as `unread > 0`, so a count of zero shows nothing instead of a stray 0.

resources.note: Rendering arrays with `map` and `filter`, and the rules for keys, with a clear picture of why they matter.
Early returns, the ternary and `&&`, including the 0 trap.
Its product table is a filtered, keyed list built step by step.

topics.title: useState and event handlers
topics.why: Every button, toggle, modal, tab and input
topics.summary: Give components memory with useState, respond to clicks and typing with event handlers, and update state the way React expects.
objectives: Add state with `useState`, and change it from event handlers such as `onClick` and `onChange`
Explain why state is a snapshot, and use the updater form when the next value depends on the last
Update objects and arrays in state by copying them, never by changing them in place

examples.title: The updater form
examples.takeaway: Each updater gets the latest queued value, so three of them add three. `setCount(count + 1)` three times would add one.

examples.title: A controlled input
examples.takeaway: `value` comes from state and `onChange` writes it back, so the input and the greeting always agree, and the greeting is derived, not stored.

examples.title: Adding to and changing an array in state
examples.takeaway: Adding spreads the old array into a new one, and toggling maps to a new array with one new object: React sees new references and renders again.

resources.note: Why ordinary variables are not enough, and how `useState` works.
Event handlers, passing them as props, and stopping default actions.
The snapshot model, step by step, and why `setCount(count + 1)` three times adds one.
Every copying pattern for arrays in state, next to the mutating one it replaces.
An illustrated guide to what makes React render again, and what doesn’t.

examples.title: Set up, clean up
examples.takeaway: The cleanup undoes exactly what the effect started: without it, every visit to the page would leave another interval running.

examples.title: Subscribe to a browser event

examples.title: You might not need an effect
examples.takeaway: A value calculated from props needs no effect and no state: calculate it while rendering, and it can never be stale.
